The 'glass transition temperature' is a complex topic in condensed matter physics — Phil Anderson and others have argued it represents the deepest unsolved problem in physics.

question: Stephanie Kwolek (DuPont chemist, 1923-2014) discovered Kevlar in 1965 while working on lightweight fibers to replace steel in tires. She produced an unusual cloudy polymer solution that, when spun, formed fibers stronger than steel by weight. Kevlar is now used in bulletproof vests (which have saved over 3,000 lives in U.S. law enforcement), tires, fiber-optic cables, and aerospace components. Her career illustrates:
answer: Major industrial breakthroughs come from sustained chemical curiosity — Kwolek noted the odd liquid
choices: Major industrial breakthroughs come from sustained chemical curiosity — Kwolek noted the odd liquid
Industrial chemistry has been entirely replaced by computer-based molecular design without lab work
Kwolek's Kevlar discovery was actually made by male DuPont chemists who got proper credit elsewhere
Aramid fibers were known since the 1920s; Kwolek's role was only commercial scaling, not discovery
context: Kwolek was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 1995. She never patented Kevlar personally — DuPont owned the patent. She earned ~$2 million in royalties over her career while DuPont made billions from Kevlar. Her story is a complex one about industrial science, patent practice, and recognition. She continued working for DuPont until retirement in 1986.

question: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren (Perth, Australia) proposed in 1984 that peptic ulcers were caused by Helicobacter pylori bacteria rather than stress or spicy food. The medical establishment dismissed this — stomach acid was thought to sterilize the gut. Marshall, frustrated by years of skepticism, drank a culture of H. pylori himself in 1984. What happened?
answer: He developed gastritis within a week — proving causation; he was treated, recovered, won 2005 Nobel
choices: He developed gastritis within a week — proving causation; he was treated, recovered, won 2005 Nobel
Marshall died from the self-experiment in 1985; Warren completed the work alone for the eventual Nobel
Nothing happened to Marshall; the experiment proved H. pylori is harmless and ulcer theory was wrong
Marshall faked the self-experiment and the 2005 Nobel was eventually retracted by the Karolinska Institute
context: Marshall said: 'There was a lot of skepticism, including hostility, and my fellow gastroenterologists thought I was nuts.' Modern peptic ulcer treatment uses antibiotics — saving ~$1 billion/year in unnecessary acid-suppression drugs and improving outcomes dramatically. The Marshall pattern (dissent → self-experimentation → vindication) parallels Semmelweis (rejected, died institutionalized; vindicated posthumously) and the GBD signatories (Bhattacharya now NIH Director).

question: Gregor Mendel (1822-1884), Augustinian friar at the Abbey of Brno (modern Czech Republic), published his pea-plant breeding experiments in 1866 in an obscure local journal. He had bred ~28,000 pea plants over eight years, deriving the laws of segregation and independent assortment. His paper was ignored for 34 years. What rediscovered Mendel's work?
answer: Three botanists (Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, Erich von Tschermak) independently rediscovered him in 1900
choices: Three botanists (Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, Erich von Tschermak) independently rediscovered him in 1900
Charles Darwin found Mendel's 1866 paper in his Down House library in 1882 just before his own death
The Catholic Church published Mendel's collected works as a sainthood case after he died in 1884
Mendel's findings were widely known and used continuously by all 19th-century plant breeders worldwide
context: Mendel sent his paper to Karl Wilhelm von Nägeli — who corresponded with him for years without grasping the work. After becoming abbot in 1868, Mendel had less time for science. His work was published in the Brünner Naturforschender Verein. The 1900 rediscovery launched modern genetics. The synthesis with Darwin (the 'modern evolutionary synthesis,' ~1930-1950, by Dobzhansky, Mayr, Simpson, others) unified evolution and genetics.

question: The Tuskegee Syphilis Study, conducted by the U.S. Public Health Service from 1932 to 1972, enrolled ~600 African American men in rural Alabama — 399 with latent syphilis, 201 without. The men were told they were being treated for 'bad blood' and given placebos. Penicillin became the standard syphilis treatment in 1947. What did the PHS do about treatment?
answer: They actively withheld penicillin from infected men — the study continued 25 more years until 1972
choices: They actively withheld penicillin from infected men — the study continued 25 more years until 1972
All study participants were given penicillin in 1947 immediately upon its becoming the standard treatment
The study was halted in 1948 when investigators realized penicillin made the research unethical to continue
Half of the men received penicillin while half received placebo as part of the original research protocol
context: Associated Press reporter Jean Heller broke the story July 25, 1972, ending the study. By then, 28 men had died of syphilis, 100 of complications, 40 wives had been infected, and 19 children were born with congenital syphilis. President Clinton issued a formal apology in 1997. The study profoundly affected African American trust in medical research and public health systems — effects measurable in vaccine hesitancy decades later. Tuskegee is the central reference point for U.S. research ethics history.

question: Buck v. Bell (274 U.S. 200, 1927) is the U.S. Supreme Court decision upholding Virginia's compulsory sterilization law. Carrie Buck, a 17-year-old woman in the Virginia State Colony for Epileptics and Feebleminded, was selected as a test case for the law. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. wrote the 8-1 majority opinion. His most notorious sentence:
answer: 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough' — based on fraudulent psychological evaluations of the Bucks
choices: 'Three generations of imbeciles are enough' — based on fraudulent psychological evaluations of the Bucks
Holmes wrote that the state could never sterilize anyone without informed consent under any circumstances
Holmes specifically rejected the legitimacy of eugenic reasoning in his published Supreme Court opinion
The opinion has been formally overturned by the Supreme Court many times since the original 1927 ruling
context: Buck v. Bell has NEVER been formally overturned. ~70,000 Americans were forcibly sterilized; California alone sterilized ~20,000. Paul Lombardo's 'Three Generations, No Imbeciles' (2008) documents the fraudulent testing. Carrie Buck's daughter Vivian (the third generation) had been doing well in school. Nazi Germany's 1933 sterilization law cited Buck v. Bell as precedent. The 1947 Nuremberg Code's voluntary-consent requirement is in direct response to such state-imposed medical violations.

question: The Human Genome Project completed a 'rough draft' in 2000 and the final sequence in 2003 — 13 years and ~$2.7 billion for the public consortium led by Francis Collins, plus parallel private work led by Craig Venter at Celera. The result was both more and less than expected. Most surprising finding:
answer: Only ~20,000 protein-coding genes — fewer than expected, similar count to mouse and worm
choices: Only ~20,000 protein-coding genes — fewer than expected, similar count to mouse and worm
Humans have over 200,000 protein-coding genes — vastly more than any other species ever studied
The Human Genome Project found no genes at all; coding regions were absent from human DNA entirely
Sequencing showed humans are genetically identical to chimpanzees with no detectable DNA differences
context: Pre-project estimates had ranged 50,000-150,000 genes. Most of the human genome is non-coding — once dismissed as 'junk DNA,' now known to contain regulatory elements, RNA genes, and complex transposable elements. The ENCODE project (2003-2012) extensively characterized non-coding regions. Total human genome size ~3.2 billion base pairs. Cost per genome has fallen from ~$3 billion in 2003 to <$1,000 today — Moore's Law for DNA sequencing.

question: Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) is the U.S. passive surveillance system for vaccine adverse events, run by CDC and FDA since 1990. Anyone can submit a report; the system is intended to detect signals warranting further investigation. What is the major limitation revealed by Harvard Pilgrim's 2010 study?
answer: VAERS captures less than 1% of actual vaccine adverse events — passive reporting drastically undercounts
choices: VAERS captures less than 1% of actual vaccine adverse events — passive reporting drastically undercounts
VAERS overstates vaccine harms by 1000% due to malicious false reports from anti-vaccine activists primarily
VAERS is a perfect record of all vaccine adverse events with no underreporting or false reports recorded
VAERS was discontinued in 2015 after being found unreliable; the U.S. now has no vaccine safety surveillance
context: The Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Study (Lazarus et al., 2010, AHRQ-funded) developed an automated reporting system. They found ~35% of VAERS reports were submitted out of ~2.6% of vaccine adverse events identified electronically — implying ~99% underreporting overall. CDC's response to Harvard Pilgrim's offer to integrate the system was unhelpful, and the system was never deployed broadly. VAERS plus the Vaccine Safety Datalink remain the primary U.S. surveillance.

question: The U.S. National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act of 1986 (NCVIA) was passed in response to a litigation crisis that threatened the U.S. childhood vaccine supply. It created the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) and provided manufacturers with substantial liability protection. The legislation's key consequence:
answer: Manufacturer liability for routine childhood vaccines was largely shielded — affecting market incentives
choices: Manufacturer liability for routine childhood vaccines was largely shielded — affecting market incentives
All vaccine manufacturers were nationalized by the U.S. government and now operate as public agencies
Vaccine manufacturers became fully liable in tort court for all vaccine injuries without exception always
The Act required vaccine manufacturers to obtain individual consent from every patient for every dose given
context: VICP is funded by a $0.75 excise tax per vaccine dose. The HHS Secretary publishes a 'Vaccine Injury Table' of presumed-causal injuries. Cases not on the table require proving causation. The CDC childhood vaccine schedule expanded from ~11 doses in 1986 to ~70+ doses by age 18 in 2025. Whether the liability shield affected pharmaceutical incentives for safety testing of the whole schedule is widely debated — and whole-schedule safety studies have not been conducted by U.S. regulators.

question: Jonas Salk (1914-1995) developed the first inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), with field trials in 1954 demonstrating efficacy. He refused to patent the vaccine: when Edward R. Murrow asked who owned the patent, Salk replied 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?' Albert Sabin (1906-1993) developed an oral live attenuated polio vaccine (OPV), used worldwide for decades. The Salk patent decision:
answer: Forfeited substantial wealth — modern observers estimate $7 billion in potential royalties given up
choices: Forfeited substantial wealth — modern observers estimate $7 billion in potential royalties given up
Was reversed by Salk himself in 1970 when he sought patent protection for revised formulations
Salk did patent the polio vaccine and earned ~$50 million in personal royalties over his lifetime
Was a non-issue: 1950s patent law did not allow patenting of biological products in the United States
context: Salk's gift contrasts sharply with modern pharma practice. The 1956 worldwide polio epidemic; the 1960s polio eradication push; Rotary International's 1985 'Polio Plus' campaign — all built on vaccines kept free of patent constraints. Polio is now nearly eradicated globally; pockets remain in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The Salk Institute (San Diego, 1960) was founded with money from the March of Dimes; it became one of the world's leading biomedical research institutes.

question: Diederik Stapel, a Dutch social psychologist at Tilburg University, was caught fabricating data in 2011. Over a decade, he had published ~50 papers in major journals using made-up data. His confession led to the retraction of 58 papers. The Stapel case was:
answer: One of social psychology's largest fraud scandals — illustrates failures of peer review and replication
choices: One of social psychology's largest fraud scandals — illustrates failures of peer review and replication
Quickly resolved without affecting confidence in social psychology research more broadly worldwide
Stapel was eventually exonerated after a 2018 review found his data had been authentic throughout
A small minor issue involving only one paper that was retracted quickly after publication problems noted
context: Stapel admitted to fabricating data for years; his Tilburg colleagues had grown suspicious as student researchers found his 'data' implausibly clean. The case was part of social psychology's broader replication crisis: Daryl Bem's 2011 'precognition' paper (extrasensory perception via published statistical effects), Amy Cuddy's 'power posing' work, the 'priming' studies that largely failed to replicate. The 2015 Open Science Collaboration confirmed many social psych findings did not reproduce.

question: Henrietta Lacks was a Black American woman from rural Virginia who died of cervical cancer in 1951 at Johns Hopkins. Without her knowledge or consent, her tumor cells were taken and cultured by George Gey. The 'HeLa' cell line — the first immortal human cell line — has been propagated worldwide for ~70 years and used in millions of experiments. Ethical issues:
answer: Family was not informed for decades; no consent given; family received no compensation until 2020s
choices: Family was not informed for decades; no consent given; family received no compensation until 2020s
The Lacks family received over $100 million in royalties from the use of HeLa cells worldwide since 1951
Mrs. Lacks gave full informed consent to research use of her cells before her death from cancer
Modern HeLa cell research has been completely halted out of respect for the family's stated concerns
context: Rebecca Skloot's 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks' (2010) brought widespread public attention. HeLa cells were used in polio vaccine development, HIV research, cancer research, and the Human Genome Project. In 2013, the NIH worked with the Lacks family on access controls for HeLa genomic data. In 2023, Thermo Fisher Scientific reached a settlement with the family. The case raised foundational issues about biospecimen consent, race, and benefit-sharing in research.

question: DDT was banned by EPA in 1972 after Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring' (1962) documented harm to wildlife (especially raptors via eggshell thinning). The ban applied to U.S. uses; international malaria-control DDT use under WHO continued. Malaria deaths in Africa:
answer: Rose substantially in some regions after DDT bans — trade-off debate continues among public health experts
choices: Rose substantially in some regions after DDT bans — trade-off debate continues among public health experts
Were completely eradicated worldwide by 1980 despite the DDT ban through alternative interventions alone
Were unaffected by DDT availability; the chemical had no impact on malaria transmission anywhere ever
The DDT ban was reversed in 2002 globally and indoor residual spraying resumed everywhere immediately
context: WHO's 2006 reversal endorsed indoor residual spraying (IRS) with DDT in some malaria-endemic settings — the chemical's outdoor agricultural-scale uses remain banned. The Stockholm Convention (2001) permits DDT for disease vector control. Insecticide-treated bed nets, artemisinin combination therapies, and other interventions have substantially reduced malaria globally (~50% mortality reduction since 2000), but malaria still kills ~600,000 per year, mostly children under 5. The DDT trade-off is genuinely complex.

question: Carrie Buck, the 17-year-old Virginia woman whose case was Buck v. Bell (1927), was sterilized on October 19, 1927. The state's case rested on claims of 'three generations of imbeciles' — Carrie, her mother Emma, and her daughter Vivian. Modern historical investigation has shown:
answer: All three were of normal intelligence; the testing was fraudulent — Carrie was raped, not 'feebleminded'
choices: All three were of normal intelligence; the testing was fraudulent — Carrie was raped, not 'feebleminded'
All three had severe intellectual disability — Justice Holmes's ruling was based on accurate testing
Carrie Buck recovered from her sterilization without lasting effects and lived a normal married life
The Buck v. Bell case was a hoax; Carrie Buck did not actually exist as a real legal subject
context: Carrie Buck was raped by a nephew of her foster family and gave birth to Vivian; the foster family sought to commit her to evade public scandal, choosing the institutionalization-and-sterilization path. Her sister Doris was also sterilized without being informed (until decades later). Paul Lombardo's 'Three Generations, No Imbeciles' (2008) is the definitive historical investigation. The story is a tragic example of how state power and pseudo-scientific authority combined to harm individuals.

question: Hwang Woo-suk (South Korean stem cell researcher) was a national hero who claimed in 2004-2005 to have created the first human embryonic stem cell lines from cloned embryos. The work was published in Science. By late 2005, the data were found to be:
answer: Fabricated — Hwang was convicted of embezzlement and falsifying research; Science retracted the papers
choices: Fabricated — Hwang was convicted of embezzlement and falsifying research; Science retracted the papers
All confirmed by independent replication studies in 2010 — Hwang's reputation was fully restored eventually
Slightly inaccurate but generally correct; the papers were corrected rather than retracted in 2006
Hwang received a Nobel Prize in 2010 after the controversy was resolved in his favor by global investigation
context: The case was a major international scientific fraud — Hwang had egg donors who were coerced, used university funds inappropriately, and fabricated data. He served a 2-year suspended sentence. His career has continued in animal cloning at lower profile. The Hwang fraud is one of the most studied cases in recent research-integrity literature; it shows how prestigious journals (Science) and major universities (Seoul National University) can fail to detect even substantial fraud when motivated reasoning aligns with national prestige.

question: The 'Little Ice Age' (~1300-1850 CE) saw cooler temperatures across Europe, North America, and parts of the world. The Maunder Minimum (1645-1715) — a period of nearly no sunspot activity — coincided with the coldest period. The Thames froze regularly. The Vikings abandoned Greenland. What does this teach about climate?
answer: Solar variability significantly affects climate; the Sun is a major driver alongside other factors
choices: Solar variability significantly affects climate; the Sun is a major driver alongside other factors
Solar output has no measurable effect on Earth's climate at any timescale or magnitude
The Little Ice Age was a fictional period invented by climate skeptics to undermine global warming science
Only volcanic activity affects climate; solar variability is negligible compared to volcanism's effects
context: Solar irradiance varies ~0.1% over the 11-year sunspot cycle; longer-term variations may be larger (debated). The Maunder Minimum (1645-1715) and Dalton Minimum (~1790-1830) both correlate with cooler periods. Modeling exact solar contribution is complex — irradiance, UV variations, solar wind effects on cosmic rays and cloud formation (Svensmark hypothesis), and magnetic-field effects all matter. Solar variability remains an active area of climate science; the establishment view weighs it as smaller than CO₂ forcing for the recent warming.

question: Climate predictions failures (those that can be checked against subsequent observations) are part of the honest scientific record. The Arctic ice-free predictions: Al Gore in 2007 said the Arctic ice cap could be ice-free by ~2013 (~7-year horizon). Scientists at NOAA, NASA, and academic institutions made similar predictions for 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2018, 2020. The actual outcomes:
answer: Arctic sea ice has declined substantially since 1979 but remains very far from ice-free in summer
choices: Arctic sea ice has declined substantially since 1979 but remains very far from ice-free in summer
Arctic sea ice has actually expanded substantially since 1979 contradicting all warming model predictions
The Arctic has been ice-free in summer since 2014 as predicted, fully validating the Gore-NOAA scenarios
Arctic sea ice cannot be measured reliably; no data on its extent exists for the recent decades period
context: September Arctic sea ice minimum (2024): ~4.3 million km² — substantially below the 1979-2010 average (~6.4 million km²) but very far from zero. The Arctic has warmed faster than the global average (~4× faster, called 'Arctic amplification'). The ice-free Arctic predictions were premature; the underlying warming is real. The pattern matters: even when underlying physics is correct, time-bounded predictions can be wrong, and admitting this is part of scientific honesty.

question: Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from ~280 ppm (pre-industrial) to ~420 ppm (2024) — an increase of ~50%. Plants use CO₂ in photosynthesis. The effect of rising CO₂ on plant growth has been measured extensively. The dominant effect:
answer: Plant growth is enhanced — measurable 'greening of the Earth' since 1980, partly from CO₂ fertilization
choices: Plant growth is enhanced — measurable 'greening of the Earth' since 1980, partly from CO₂ fertilization
CO₂ has no effect on plant growth; photosynthesis is determined entirely by light and water alone
All plant growth has decreased substantially due to atmospheric CO₂ increases destroying photosynthesis chemistry
Only invasive weed species benefit from CO₂; food crops show no measurable growth enhancement
context: Zhu et al. 2016 (Nature Climate Change) documented global greening of ~25-50% of Earth's vegetated land surfaces since 1980, attributing ~70% to CO₂ fertilization. Effects on specific crops: ~5-30% yield enhancement at doubled CO₂ for C3 plants (most crops). However, CO₂ fertilization may reduce nutrient density (zinc, iron, protein); warming and altered precipitation may offset growth benefits. The full picture is complex; CO₂'s direct biological effect is a real and measurable benefit for plant growth.

question: Earth's magnetic field — generated by liquid iron-nickel convection in the outer core — has reversed direction ~183 times in the past 83 million years. The last reversal (Brunhes-Matuyama) was ~780,000 years ago. The current field has been weakening ~5% per century. What might a reversal cause?
answer: Increased cosmic ray flux during weakened field — possible electrical/biological effects, well-studied
choices: Increased cosmic ray flux during weakened field — possible electrical/biological effects, well-studied
Catastrophic global warming as solar radiation increases by orders of magnitude across the entire planet
Spontaneous reversal of Earth's rotation direction with day becoming night for a sustained period
Magnetic-field reversals are entirely fictional and have never actually occurred in Earth's geological history
context: Field reversals take ~1,000-10,000 years and involve a period of weakened field; cosmic radiation rises during this period. The biological impact is unclear from past reversals; mass extinctions don't track reversals well. The South Atlantic Anomaly — a region of weakened field over South America and the South Atlantic — has been growing, causing problems for satellites. The earlier Laschamp event (~41,000 years ago) was a brief field weakening; some have linked it to Neanderthal extinction (controversial).

question: El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the largest natural year-to-year climate variation. El Niño phases (warmer eastern Pacific) bring drought to Australia, Indonesia; heavier rainfall to Peru, southern US. La Niña phases have opposite effects. The 1997-1998 'Super El Niño':
answer: Was the largest in instrumental record at the time — caused 'pause' in subsequent global temperature rise
choices: Was the largest in instrumental record at the time — caused 'pause' in subsequent global temperature rise
Had no measurable effect on global temperature averages or regional climate patterns globally
Was the only such event in recorded history; ENSO has never repeated since 1998 to today
Cooled Earth substantially for the next two decades counteracting all anthropogenic warming entirely
context: ENSO timescale ~2-7 years; physical mechanism involves trade-wind weakening, Kelvin and Rossby waves in the Pacific. The 1997-1998 El Niño raised global temperatures temporarily; the 'pause' or 'hiatus' (~2000-2015) in warming followed and was widely debated. The 2015-2016 El Niño was equally strong; the 2023-2024 El Niño helped push global temperatures to records. ENSO matters because it's a natural variation comparable in magnitude to a decade of anthropogenic warming.

question: On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility. Armstrong's first words: 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind' (the 'a' is debated, possibly lost in transmission). The total cost of the Apollo Program (1961-1972):
answer: ~$25 billion in 1973 dollars (~$170 billion in 2024 dollars) — ~4% of US federal budget at peak
choices: ~$25 billion in 1973 dollars (~$170 billion in 2024 dollars) — ~4% of US federal budget at peak
Approximately $10 million total cost — far less than commonly reported in mainstream historical accounts
Approximately $1 trillion in current dollars; the Apollo Program nearly bankrupted the U.S. economically
Apollo's exact total cost is classified and has never been disclosed by NASA or the U.S. government
context: Apollo employed ~400,000 people at peak. The Saturn V rocket — 363 ft tall, 6.5 million pounds at launch — remains one of humanity's great engineering achievements. The political backdrop: Kennedy's May 1961 commitment (after Soviet first-human-in-space Gagarin); Cold War prestige; Cold War demonstration of US technological capability. Apollo 11 mission patched the U.S. space program's psychological need; the subsequent missions (Apollo 12-17 except 13) brought back ~382 kg of lunar samples that still drive lunar science.

question: Apollo Moon landing conspiracy theories date from 1976 (Bill Kaysing's 'We Never Went to the Moon'). They claim the landings were faked in studios. Direct scientific responses:
answer: Lunar retroreflectors still bounce laser pulses; ~382 kg of samples; multiple independent country verifications
choices: Lunar retroreflectors still bounce laser pulses; ~382 kg of samples; multiple independent country verifications
Conspiracy theorists have proven their claims; the Moon landings did not actually happen in 1969
No scientific evidence exists that the landings occurred; the entire program was a Cold War simulation only
The Apollo missions were partially faked; only some Moon landings happened in reality
context: The Apollo missions placed retroreflectors on the Moon that observatories worldwide still use for laser-ranging measurements (precision distance to Moon ~1 mm). Independent verification includes Soviet Lunokhod samples + Chang'e samples and analysis of Apollo lunar rocks by laboratories in dozens of countries. Buzz Aldrin (an MIT astronautical engineer with a PhD in orbital mechanics) famously punched Bart Sibrel in 2002 after being harassed on camera over conspiracy claims. The conspiracy theories illustrate how confidence intervals about a known event widen with cultural distance.

question: Voyager 1 (launched September 5, 1977) is the most distant human-made object — currently ~24 billion km from Earth, in interstellar space (entered August 25, 2012). Its plutonium-238 power supply will last until ~2030. Voyager 1's most striking image was the 'Pale Blue Dot':
answer: Earth photographed from 6 billion km on February 14, 1990 at Carl Sagan's request
choices: Earth photographed from 6 billion km on February 14, 1990 at Carl Sagan's request
Detailed close-up of Mars surface taken in 2010 by the rover instruments under Voyager mission control
Pluto's surface from a 1995 flyby that revealed mountains and possible liquid nitrogen lakes on the dwarf planet
An image of Proxima Centauri from 2018 showing the first directly imaged exoplanet in another star system
context: Sagan wrote: 'Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us...The aggregate of our joy and suffering, thousands of confident religions, ideologies, and economic doctrines, every hunter and forager, every hero and coward...lived there.' Voyager 1 carries the Golden Record — a phonograph record with sounds and images of Earth, intended for any extraterrestrial intelligence that might find it. The record has greetings in 55 languages plus sounds of nature, music (Bach, Berry, Pakistani Surshringar), and brain waves.

question: James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror is 6.5 meters in diameter — vs. Hubble's 2.4 meters. JWST observes primarily in infrared, can see further back in cosmic history than Hubble (~13.5 billion years ago). The launch (December 25, 2021) was preceded by:
answer: ~25 years of development, multiple delays, cost overrun from $1B to ~$10B — successful deployment
choices: ~25 years of development, multiple delays, cost overrun from $1B to ~$10B — successful deployment
Approximately one year of development and on-budget completion below the original $1 billion estimate
JWST has not actually launched; the project was canceled in 2018 due to escalating cost concerns
JWST replaced Hubble immediately after Hubble's 1990 launch; the missions overlapped for many decades
context: JWST's deployment involved ~344 single points of failure (any one of which could have ended the mission). The 18-segment primary mirror unfolded successfully. JWST orbits the L2 Lagrange point ~1.5 million km from Earth (vs. Hubble in low Earth orbit). The mission has produced unexpectedly bright high-redshift galaxies (z~10-14), atmospheric spectra of exoplanets, and the deepest infrared images ever obtained. JWST is one of the most successful astronomical instruments in history; the cost overruns and delays were real but the outcome justified the investment.

question: Sea level rise is one of climate change's most-discussed consequences. Global mean sea level has risen ~21-24 cm since 1880. The current rate (~3.4 mm/year average, ~4-5 mm/year recently from satellite altimetry). Components of rise:
answer: Thermal expansion (~1/3); melting ice (Greenland, Antarctica, glaciers, ~2/3); ice loss is accelerating
choices: Thermal expansion (~1/3); melting ice (Greenland, Antarctica, glaciers, ~2/3); ice loss is accelerating
Continental sinking accounts for all sea-level rise; ice and ocean volumes are completely stable globally
Sea level has actually been falling since 1900 by ~1 mm/year contradicting the climate concern narrative
Sea-level rise is impossible to measure reliably; no scientific data on the topic exists currently
context: Greenland ice loss: ~280 Gt/year (2002-2023); Antarctica: ~150 Gt/year (accelerating, with West Antarctic Ice Sheet most at risk). The IPCC AR6 projects 0.28-1.01 m of additional rise by 2100 across scenarios. Coastal infrastructure adaptation costs are real and growing. Low-lying island nations (Maldives, Tuvalu) face existential threat — but media predictions of imminent submersion have repeatedly failed. The Maldives has actually grown in land area in some recent decades despite sea-level rise.

question: Greenland's ice sheet contains enough water to raise global sea level ~7.4 meters if entirely melted. Modeling suggests this could occur over many centuries if global temperatures rise sufficiently. Current rate of ice loss:
answer: Variable year to year; 2012 and 2019 were particularly high-loss years; trend is overall toward loss
choices: Variable year to year; 2012 and 2019 were particularly high-loss years; trend is overall toward loss
Greenland is actually gaining ice at a rate of 1000 cubic km per year contradicting all warming concerns
Greenland's entire ice sheet has already melted as of 2023 raising sea levels by 7.4 meters worldwide
Greenland ice changes cannot be measured; no satellite or ground data exists for the polar regions
context: GRACE and GRACE-Follow-On satellite gravity measurements (2002-present) provide direct ice mass estimates. Surface mass balance (snow accumulation minus melt) plus glacier discharge (calving) together give net change. Greenland's coastal glaciers have accelerated as warm ocean water erodes them from below. The 'tipping point' question — past which Greenland melt becomes self-reinforcing — is a real concern; estimates of threshold temperatures range from 1.5°C to 3°C of warming.

question: The Antarctic ozone hole — discovered by Joe Farman et al. (British Antarctic Survey) in 1985 — covers ~22 million km² each spring. The 1987 Montreal Protocol banned CFCs to address it. The ozone hole's current trajectory:
answer: Shrinking — projected to fully recover ~2060-2080 if Montreal Protocol compliance continues
choices: Shrinking — projected to fully recover ~2060-2080 if Montreal Protocol compliance continues
Has been continuously growing despite the Montreal Protocol; CFC bans had no effect on ozone chemistry
Completely recovered by 2000 and ozone-related concerns are not in scientific literature anymore today
Never actually existed; the 1985 ozone hole observation was a measurement artifact later refuted
context: WMO/UNEP 'Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion 2022' projected Antarctic ozone hole recovery to 1980 levels by ~2066. NASA reports the September 2023 ozone hole was the 12th-largest on record — interannual variability remains substantial. The Antarctic ozone hole is a clear example of successful global environmental cooperation: identifiable industries, viable substitutes, visible problem, treaty enforcement, monitoring infrastructure. The factors that made Montreal work are mostly absent from CO₂ politics.

question: Mid-ocean ridges are seafloor mountain chains where new oceanic crust forms. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs ~16,000 km from the Arctic to Antarctica; the East Pacific Rise is similar. New seafloor forms at ~2-15 cm/year. The first direct evidence:
answer: Magnetic stripe patterns parallel to ridges (Vine-Matthews 1963) match Earth's magnetic field reversal record
choices: Magnetic stripe patterns parallel to ridges (Vine-Matthews 1963) match Earth's magnetic field reversal record
Direct visual observation by deep-sea submersibles in the 1850s confirmed seafloor spreading immediately
Mid-ocean ridges do not exist; the seafloor is completely flat and uniform across all ocean basins
Seafloor spreading has been discredited; modern geology rejects plate tectonics theory entirely after 2000
context: Frederick Vine and Drummond Matthews (1963 Nature paper) showed seafloor magnetic anomalies are symmetric across mid-ocean ridges and match the timing of Earth's magnetic-field reversals (recorded in volcanic rocks). The pattern proved seafloor spreading is real and continuous. Combined with subduction zones (Wadati-Benioff zones) and continental drift, plate tectonics became the unifying theory of geology. The acceptance of plate tectonics (~1965-1970) is one of science's clearest examples of a paradigm shift — Wegener was vindicated 50 years posthumously.

question: The first exoplanet (planet orbiting another star) was confirmed in 1992 (Wolszczan and Frail, around pulsar PSR B1257+12). The first planet around a Sun-like star (51 Pegasi b) was confirmed in 1995 by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz (2019 Nobel). The current count of confirmed exoplanets (2025):
answer: ~5,800 confirmed planets across ~4,300 planetary systems — most discovered via Kepler and TESS missions
choices: ~5,800 confirmed planets across ~4,300 planetary systems — most discovered via Kepler and TESS missions
Approximately 50 confirmed exoplanets total; the field has not advanced significantly since the 1990s
Approximately 10 million confirmed exoplanets; nearly every star has multiple confirmed planetary systems orbiting
Exoplanets are theoretical; no planet outside our solar system has been directly confirmed by observation
context: NASA's Kepler Space Telescope (2009-2018) used transit photometry to find planets by their tiny dips in starlight when they cross their host star. TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched 2018) continues. Most stars have planets; many have 'habitable zone' planets where liquid water could exist. The question 'are we alone in the universe?' has shifted from philosophy to active observation. Astrobiology (the search for life beyond Earth) is a major emerging discipline.

question: Solar power has scaled rapidly since 2000 — global installed capacity grew from ~1 GW (2000) to ~1,700 GW (2024). Cost per kWh has fallen ~90% — solar is now competitive with or cheaper than coal in many markets. Major remaining challenges:
answer: Intermittency — sun doesn't shine at night/cloudy; storage (batteries, pumped hydro) is the bottleneck
choices: Intermittency — sun doesn't shine at night/cloudy; storage (batteries, pumped hydro) is the bottleneck
Solar power has been completely abandoned worldwide because it cannot produce useful electricity at all
Solar power produces unlimited stored energy without any intermittency or storage challenges to overcome
Solar panels themselves are now too expensive for any commercial deployment despite decades of research
context: Lithium-ion battery costs have fallen ~90% since 2010 — driving electric vehicle and grid-storage growth. Vanadium and sodium-ion flow batteries are emerging for stationary storage. Pumped hydro remains the largest existing grid storage. Nuclear power's role in a decarbonized grid remains contested — France's mostly nuclear grid is among the lowest-carbon in Europe. The IRA (2022) provided substantial US tax credits for solar, wind, batteries, and nuclear. Energy transition is real but harder than rhetoric often implies.

question: Saturn's largest moon Titan is the only moon in the solar system with a substantial atmosphere (1.5× Earth's surface pressure, mostly nitrogen with methane). The Huygens probe (ESA) landed on Titan on January 14, 2005 — the most distant landing in human history. What did it find?
answer: Hydrocarbon lakes, dune systems, eroded river channels — an alien Earth-like landscape with methane cycle
choices: Hydrocarbon lakes, dune systems, eroded river channels — an alien Earth-like landscape with methane cycle
Titan is a barren rocky surface identical to Earth's Moon with no atmospheric or geological features
Huygens never actually landed on Titan; the ESA mission was canceled before launch due to budget issues
Titan was found to have liquid water oceans on its surface contradicting all prior model predictions completely
context: Cassini (NASA orbiter) and Huygens (ESA descent probe) reached Saturn in 2004; Cassini operated until 2017. Titan's methane cycle (methane evaporates, forms clouds, rains, fills lakes) is the only known active hydrological cycle outside Earth. The 2027 Dragonfly mission (NASA) will fly a rotorcraft on Titan to explore its prebiotic chemistry. Titan is one of the solar system's most astrobiologically interesting bodies — the question is whether liquid hydrocarbons can support some form of chemistry analogous to water-based life.

question: Jupiter's moon Europa has an icy surface but evidence for a subsurface liquid water ocean (~100 km deep, ~2-3× Earth's total water content). The ocean is in contact with rocky seafloor and may have hydrothermal vents. NASA's Europa Clipper:
answer: Launched October 2024, will arrive at Jupiter ~April 2030 to study Europa's habitability extensively
choices: Launched October 2024, will arrive at Jupiter ~April 2030 to study Europa's habitability extensively
Was canceled in 2022 due to budget overruns and the spacecraft was scrapped before launch attempts
Has already landed on Europa and detected microbial life under the moon's icy surface in 2018
Was lost during launch in 2024 with no further missions to Europa planned by NASA in the future
context: Europa Clipper carries a suite of instruments to study Europa's ice shell, ocean composition, geology, and potential plume activity (water erupting from cracks). NASA estimates ~50 close Europa flybys (cannot orbit Europa directly due to Jupiter's intense radiation). The mission is one of two flagship astrobiology missions of the 2020s (along with Mars Sample Return). Europa is considered among the most likely places in the solar system for extant life beyond Earth.

question: The asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter contains ~1 million objects >1 km diameter and Ceres (~940 km) is the largest. The belt's total mass is ~4% of Earth's Moon. Why didn't a planet form there?
answer: Jupiter's gravitational perturbation prevented accretion — the belt is a 'failed' planet's worth of debris
choices: Jupiter's gravitational perturbation prevented accretion — the belt is a 'failed' planet's worth of debris
The asteroid belt is actually the destroyed remains of a once-existing planet called Phaeton or similar
Asteroids are extra-solar interlopers captured by the solar system; no native planet ever formed in the region
The asteroid belt does not exist; this is a popular astronomy myth without supporting empirical evidence
context: The 'destroyed planet' (Phaeton/Olbers's planet) idea was widely popular in the 19th century but is rejected by modern dynamics. Jupiter's gravity dominates the belt's evolution — resonant orbits (Kirkwood gaps) are largely empty. Ceres is now classified as a dwarf planet. NASA's Dawn mission (2007-2018) orbited Vesta and Ceres, providing detailed maps. Most meteorites that fall on Earth originate in the asteroid belt — the 4.5-billion-year-old chemistry recorded in primitive chondrites provides crucial information about solar system formation.

question: Coral reefs are among the most biologically diverse ecosystems — covering <1% of ocean area but hosting ~25% of marine species. They are also among the most threatened by combined stressors. The IPCC AR6 projected that:
answer: Most warm-water reefs are likely to decline 70-90% at 1.5°C global warming vs. preindustrial
choices: Most warm-water reefs are likely to decline 70-90% at 1.5°C global warming vs. preindustrial
Coral reefs are expanding globally and will reach maximum coverage in the next decade with no decline
Coral reefs have been completely destroyed worldwide since 2010; none currently exist on Earth in 2025
Coral reefs have nothing to do with ocean temperature; warming has no effect on coral health at all
context: Australia's Great Barrier Reef has experienced major bleaching in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024. Reef ecosystems also face pressure from ocean acidification (decreasing pH from CO₂ absorption), pollution, sedimentation from coastal development, fishing pressure, and disease outbreaks. The IPCC's projections include real uncertainties; some reef systems may adapt or migrate while others may not. The complex picture is real concern combined with substantial scientific uncertainty about specific outcomes.

question: Ocean acidification — the decline in ocean pH from absorption of atmospheric CO₂ — has reduced ocean pH from ~8.2 (pre-industrial) to ~8.1 today. The chemistry: CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H+ + HCO₃-. Implications for marine life:
answer: Calcifying organisms (corals, shellfish, plankton) face stress; aragonite saturation drops at poles first
choices: Calcifying organisms (corals, shellfish, plankton) face stress; aragonite saturation drops at poles first
Ocean acidification has no effect on any marine organisms; the chemistry has no biological significance
Ocean acidification will completely sterilize all oceans within five years through universal toxicity
Ocean pH has not changed since 1900 contrary to widely cited but fabricated climate concern claims
context: 0.1 pH unit drop is ~30% increase in hydrogen ion concentration (pH is logarithmic). Aragonite saturation state determines whether shells can form; below saturation 1, shells dissolve faster than they form. Pacific oyster hatcheries in the Pacific Northwest experienced acidification damage in 2007-2008; they now adjust water chemistry. Many marine organisms can adapt to slow pH change but face stress from rapid change. The economic impact on shellfish industries is real and growing.

question: Glaciers worldwide have been retreating since ~1850 (end of the Little Ice Age). The rate has accelerated since ~1980. Glacial National Park in Montana had ~150 glaciers in 1850, ~25 remaining in 2025. Tropical glaciers (Andes, Africa, New Guinea) are particularly vulnerable. The complications:
answer: Some glaciers (mainly tidewater) are advancing; total mass loss is real; tipping points are concerning
choices: Some glaciers (mainly tidewater) are advancing; total mass loss is real; tipping points are concerning
All glaciers worldwide are stable and have not retreated at all since the end of the Little Ice Age
All glaciers have completely melted as of 2023; no ice remains anywhere on Earth's land surface
Glaciers have actually been advancing worldwide since 1850 contradicting all retreat measurements
context: GlaThiDa (Global Glacier Thickness Database) and satellite remote sensing provide direct measurements of glacier mass changes. Net mass loss from glaciers (excluding ice sheets): ~290 Gt/year (2000-2019). This contributes ~0.8 mm/year to sea-level rise. Some Karakoram glaciers in Pakistan are anomalously stable or advancing (the 'Karakoram anomaly,' possibly due to local precipitation patterns). Mont Blanc, Switzerland's glaciers, the Andes glaciers, Mt. Kilimanjaro — all have measurable retreat. The global pattern is real even if regional variations exist.

question: The Younger Dryas (~12,900-11,700 years ago) was a rapid cooling event — temperatures dropped ~10°C in Greenland within decades, then warmed similarly fast at the end. The cause is debated. Three leading hypotheses:
answer: Meltwater pulse disrupting AMOC; cometary impact ('Younger Dryas impact'); volcanic eruption
choices: Meltwater pulse disrupting AMOC; cometary impact ('Younger Dryas impact'); volcanic eruption
Younger Dryas was caused exclusively by human agricultural activity at the start of the Neolithic period
The Younger Dryas event never actually happened; it is a misinterpretation of Greenland ice core data
The cooling was caused entirely by an asteroid impact identical to the End-Cretaceous Chicxulub event
context: The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis (proposed Firestone et al. 2007) cites nanodiamonds, platinum, melt glass, and other markers in a layer worldwide at ~12,800 BP. The hypothesis is controversial — many archaeologists and geologists are unconvinced. The melt-pulse hypothesis (massive meltwater from glacial Lake Agassiz disrupting AMOC) has long been favored. The volcanic-eruption hypothesis (Laacher See volcano in Germany) gained traction with recent dating work. The Younger Dryas killed off North American megafauna and disrupted Clovis culture.

question: Earth's moon was likely formed by a giant impact between proto-Earth and a Mars-sized body (named 'Theia') ~4.5 billion years ago. The impact ejected material that coalesced into the Moon. Evidence for this hypothesis:
answer: Earth and Moon have similar isotopic ratios; Moon's iron-poor composition consistent with mantle ejecta
choices: Earth and Moon have similar isotopic ratios; Moon's iron-poor composition consistent with mantle ejecta
The Moon was confirmed in 1969 to have been brought from Mars by ancient extraterrestrial civilizations
The Moon's formation cannot be determined; no scientific data exists about its origin or composition
The Moon formed independently from Earth and was captured by gravitational interaction much later
context: The giant-impact hypothesis explains the Moon's composition (poor in iron, similar to Earth's mantle), the Earth-Moon system's angular momentum, and the Moon's depleted volatiles. Alternative theories (capture, co-accretion, fission) have major problems. Recent refinements: 'multiple-impact' models (several smaller impacts), 'synestia' phase (Earth and Moon both within a hot rotating disk of vaporized rock). Apollo samples revealed the Moon is depleted in volatile elements compared to Earth — consistent with high-temperature formation.

question: The 'Late Heavy Bombardment' (~4.1-3.8 billion years ago) was a proposed spike in asteroid/comet impacts on the inner solar system. Evidence came from age clustering of Moon impact basins. Recent reinterpretation:
answer: Possibly an artifact of sampling; the bombardment may have been more continuous than 'late spike'
choices: Possibly an artifact of sampling; the bombardment may have been more continuous than 'late spike'
Confirmed beyond doubt; the bombardment had ten times current asteroid impact rates exactly
The Late Heavy Bombardment never occurred; the proposal is now considered scientific pseudoscience
The bombardment is currently ongoing; impact rates today are identical to those of 4 billion years ago
context: Most Apollo samples came from the Imbrium impact basin region; the apparent age clustering may reflect Imbrium ejecta rather than a true global spike. Recent work on lunar zircons and impact-rich crust suggests the bombardment may have been declining steadily without a 'late spike.' The 'Nice Model' of solar system dynamics (proposed in 2005) postulates the bombardment was triggered by giant planet migration. The case illustrates how scientific consensus can shift with better data and analysis.

question: School closures during COVID were among the most consequential policy choices. The 'NWEA Map Growth Data' (~8 million US students) documented learning loss: ~5 months in reading, ~7 months in math. The differential impact:
answer: Poorer students fell behind most; wealthier districts often reopened sooner — equity gap widened sharply
choices: Poorer students fell behind most; wealthier districts often reopened sooner — equity gap widened sharply
School closures had no measurable effect on student learning according to all available data
School closures benefited students academically; outcomes improved during the period schools were closed entirely
All US schools remained open during the entire 2020 academic year despite some district-level restrictions
context: Stanford's Eric Hanushek estimated US school closures will cost ~$28 trillion in lifetime earnings to affected cohort. Mental health crises among adolescents (suicide, self-harm, anxiety) rose substantially during and after closures. The CDC's own 2021 paper ('Promoting Mental Health and Well-Being in Schools') acknowledged the toll. Sweden's open-schools policy was vindicated when its children's outcomes were ultimately better than locked-down peers. The case is increasingly cited as the worst public-health policy failure of COVID.

question: FDA's 'Right to Try' federal law (signed May 2018) gave terminally ill patients access to experimental drugs that have passed FDA Phase I trials but not yet final approval. The law was controversial:
answer: Strongly opposed by FDA + medical establishment as undermining approval process; libertarian supporters argued autonomy
choices: Strongly opposed by FDA + medical establishment as undermining approval process; libertarian supporters argued autonomy
Strongly supported by FDA + medical establishment as restoring patient choice; libertarian opposition was minimal
Right to Try has never been signed into US federal law; it remains only a state-level concept currently
The federal law was repealed in 2020 after being shown to harm patients more than help them medically
context: Goldwater Institute drove the 'Right to Try' campaign for years before federal passage. Critics argued the FDA's existing compassionate-use program was adequate. Supporters argued FDA delays in compassionate use were excessive; dying patients shouldn't wait for bureaucratic processes. The federal law has been used by hundreds of patients but uptake has been modest. The underlying ethical question — when is regulatory delay justifiable for terminally ill patients? — divides bioethicists. The case illustrates broader tensions between regulatory authority and patient autonomy.

question: The FDA's accelerated approval process (created 1992 for HIV drugs, expanded since) approves drugs based on 'surrogate endpoints' (e.g., tumor shrinkage) rather than survival benefit. Vinay Prasad's research:
answer: Many accelerated-approved drugs lack later confirmation of survival benefit; some are eventually withdrawn
choices: Many accelerated-approved drugs lack later confirmation of survival benefit; some are eventually withdrawn
All accelerated-approval drugs have been confirmed to provide survival benefit upon longer-term studies
The accelerated approval pathway was eliminated in 2010 and is no longer used by the FDA at all
Accelerated approval requires more evidence than standard approval; it is the most rigorous regulatory pathway
context: Prasad's 2014 paper in JAMA Internal Medicine examined cancer drugs given accelerated approval — many subsequently failed to demonstrate survival benefit. The 'industry capture' critique applies: drug companies have substantial incentives to push for accelerated approval; patients want access; the FDA approves; subsequent rigorous trials are sometimes never completed. The aducanumab (Aduhelm) controversy 2021 — FDA approved Alzheimer's drug over advisory committee 0-10 rejection — is a recent example. Patient hope and corporate marketing can drive approvals beyond rigorous evidence support.

question: Pfizer's 2009 settlement with the US Department of Justice (~$2.3 billion) included a guilty plea for illegally marketing Bextra (off-label promotion of pain reliever, which had been withdrawn from the market in 2005). The case set a:
answer: Then-record pharma criminal settlement; pattern of repeated DOJ settlements with same companies continues
choices: Then-record pharma criminal settlement; pattern of repeated DOJ settlements with same companies continues
First and only criminal settlement Pfizer has ever paid; the company has been compliant since 2009 entirely
Pfizer was completely exonerated of all charges in 2010 and the settlement was reversed unanimously
Pfizer is a non-profit organization that has never been involved in any legal proceedings in its history
context: The 2009 Pfizer settlement was historic but unfortunately not unique. Pharmaceutical industry repeated settlements include: GlaxoSmithKline $3 billion (2012), Pfizer $2.3 billion (2009), AbbVie $1.6 billion (Humira), Johnson & Johnson $2.2 billion (2013), Purdue Pharma $8 billion (2020), and many others. Critics argue these settlements are factored into business models — they represent 'cost of doing business' rather than meaningful deterrent. The pattern of repeated criminal/civil violations by major pharma companies is part of the regulatory-capture analysis.

question: Direct-to-consumer pharmaceutical advertising is legal only in the US and New Zealand. The US Supreme Court's Virginia State Pharmacy Board v. Virginia Citizens Consumer Council (1976) granted First Amendment protection to commercial speech, paving the way for DTC drug ads. The annual US DTC drug ad spending:
answer: ~$10 billion in 2024 — exceeds spending on pharmaceutical research-and-development in some major companies
choices: ~$10 billion in 2024 — exceeds spending on pharmaceutical research-and-development in some major companies
Approximately $100 million; DTC advertising is a small fraction of pharmaceutical marketing budgets historically
DTC pharmaceutical advertising has been banned in the United States since 2010 with no exceptions today
All US pharmaceutical advertising must focus exclusively on side effects with no efficacy claims allowed
context: DTC ads contributed to the over-prescription of opioids, ADHD medications, antidepressants, and many other drug classes. The 'Ask Your Doctor If X Is Right For You' marketing has been criticized as inducing demand. Multiple US states have considered DTC advertising restrictions; federal action has been limited. The American Medical Association has formally called for DTC ad restrictions. Critics argue patient autonomy is undermined by mass marketing for symptoms that may not require pharmaceutical intervention. The industry argues information access serves patients.

question: PDUFA (Prescription Drug User Fee Act, 1992 + renewals) created an industry-funded FDA review system. Drug companies pay 'user fees' to fund FDA review; the FDA now receives ~70% of drug-review funding from industry. Defenders argue:
answer: Faster approval, more new drugs reaching patients; industry investment in robust review process
choices: Faster approval, more new drugs reaching patients; industry investment in robust review process
Industry funding has no measurable effect on FDA review timelines or approval rates at any level
PDUFA was repealed in 2005 and the FDA returned to entirely taxpayer-funded operations with no industry inputs
PDUFA only applies to over-the-counter products; prescription drug reviews are completely industry-independent
context: Critics (Vinay Prasad, Aaron Kheriaty, Sidney Wolfe, Public Citizen, others) argue PDUFA structurally compromises FDA independence — the agency's customer is the drug company paying for review, not the patient. Approval rates have indeed risen post-PDUFA; whether approved drugs are appropriately safer/more effective is debated. The 'fee for service' model is unusual for safety regulators; consider whether airline crash investigators should be paid by airlines. The structural conflict-of-interest analysis is straightforward; the empirical question of impact on actual decisions is more complex.

question: Paul Ehrlich's 'Population Bomb' (1968) predicted: 'In the 1970s and 1980s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death in spite of any crash programs embarked upon now.' The actual outcome:
answer: Norman Borlaug's Green Revolution prevented predicted famine; global food production outpaced population growth dramatically
choices: Norman Borlaug's Green Revolution prevented predicted famine; global food production outpaced population growth dramatically
Ehrlich's predictions were exactly accurate; hundreds of millions did starve to death in the 1970s and 1980s
The 'Population Bomb' book was never actually published despite widespread media references to it currently
Ehrlich has acknowledged his predictions were entirely correct and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for them
context: Ehrlich's predictions were spectacularly wrong: global famine deaths declined from ~10 million annually pre-1968 to ~tens of thousands today. Population growth has continued (~7.8 billion in 2025) but per-capita food has improved markedly. Ehrlich won the Crafoord Prize (1990, equivalent to Nobel for some fields) and was elected to NAS — despite his predictions being demonstrably wrong. Julian Simon's $1000 bet with Ehrlich (1980-1990, on resource prices) was won by Simon. The case is the canonical example of academic celebrity surviving spectacularly failed predictions — which now arguably parallels climate alarmism.

question: DDT was banned by EPA in 1972 following Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring' (1962). The ban applied to US uses. Internationally, malaria-control DDT use continued under WHO and the Stockholm Convention (2001). The historical assessment:
answer: Carson's documentation of wildlife effects was accurate; broader claims about cancer have been substantially modified
choices: Carson's documentation of wildlife effects was accurate; broader claims about cancer have been substantially modified
Silent Spring was entirely fictional and Rachel Carson's claims have all been refuted by subsequent investigations
DDT was proven to be entirely harmless; the EPA ban has been reversed and DDT is now used widely in the US
DDT remains banned worldwide with no malaria-control exceptions allowed by any international authority currently
context: Carson's eggshell-thinning claims for raptors (eagles, peregrines, ospreys, brown pelicans) were validated; bald eagle and peregrine recoveries are real conservation successes. Her broader claims about human cancer risk have been substantially modified — DDT is now classified as a probable human carcinogen but at high doses; epidemiological evidence for typical exposures is weaker than she suggested. The 'Carson killed millions of malaria victims' narrative oversimplifies — WHO retained DDT for indoor residual spraying. The honest assessment: she was right about wildlife effects and somewhat right about cancer concerns; banning all uses internationally was probably overcorrection.

question: The Linear No-Threshold (LNT) model for radiation risk assumes any radiation dose carries proportional cancer risk; there is no 'safe' threshold. The LNT model has been the basis for radiation protection standards globally since the 1950s. Recent reassessment:
answer: Multiple studies question LNT at low doses; hormesis (low-dose benefits) is a contested but real possibility
choices: Multiple studies question LNT at low doses; hormesis (low-dose benefits) is a contested but real possibility
LNT has been definitively confirmed across all dose ranges with no scientific dispute remaining whatsoever ever
LNT has been universally abandoned by all radiation protection agencies worldwide since 2010 with no replacement
Radiation dose-response is a discredited scientific concept that has no current relevance to safety standards anywhere
context: LNT was adopted partly for regulatory simplicity (any reduction is presumed beneficial). Empirical data at low doses shows substantial scatter; hormesis (low-dose beneficial effects, demonstrated for many toxins via stress-response mechanisms) may apply to radiation. The Taiwan apartment-building case (~200,000 person-years of low-dose cobalt-60 exposure) showed lower cancer rates than the general population — suggesting hormesis. The LNT assumption substantially shaped Fukushima's evacuation policy and Chernobyl's exclusion zone. Honest reassessment is ongoing but politically charged.

question: Solar power has scaled dramatically since 2000 — global installed capacity grew from ~1 GW to ~1700 GW. Costs have fallen ~90%. Solar is now competitive with coal in many markets. The intermittency problem:
answer: Major — solar produces zero output at night and reduced output under clouds; storage is the bottleneck
choices: Major — solar produces zero output at night and reduced output under clouds; storage is the bottleneck
Solar has no intermittency problem; output is constant throughout the day and night every day everywhere
Solar produces electricity only at night through unspecified physical mechanisms not yet understood by physicists
Solar intermittency has been entirely eliminated by improved solar panel designs since the year 2010 globally
context: Lithium-ion battery costs have fallen ~90% since 2010 (~$130/kWh, projected to ~$60 by 2030). Pumped hydro remains the largest grid-scale storage. Vanadium and sodium-ion flow batteries are emerging. The 'duck curve' problem — solar overgeneration midday, ramping needed evening — is real and growing in California. Renewable energy plus storage is increasingly competitive in some applications but not yet a complete grid solution. Texas's 2021 winter blackout was a complex combination of weather, grid design, and inadequate winterization — not purely renewable failure but a real fragility lesson.

question: Wind power has scaled dramatically since 2000 (~17 GW in 2000 to ~900 GW in 2024). Offshore wind is the next frontier. Concerns:
answer: Variability; transmission requirements; wildlife (bird/bat) mortality; visual/community impact; eventual disposal
choices: Variability; transmission requirements; wildlife (bird/bat) mortality; visual/community impact; eventual disposal
Wind power is universally controversial-free with no environmental or community impact whatsoever ever
Wind power is completely banned in all developed countries due to documented severe environmental hazards
Wind turbines have unlimited operational lifespans and require no replacement or disposal at any point
context: Wind turbines kill ~500,000 birds and ~1 million bats annually in US alone (Loss et al. 2013). House cats kill ~2.4 billion birds annually — wind is small in proportion but real. Turbine blade disposal is challenging (composite materials are difficult to recycle). Modern turbines have ~20-25 year lifespans. Land use is substantial — distributed wind requires far more land than equivalent nuclear or even gas plants. The 'NIMBY' (Not In My Back Yard) opposition to wind projects is real even among climate-concerned populations. Wind is part of the energy transition but with real trade-offs.

question: Public trust in science has declined substantially in the US since the 2010s, particularly post-COVID. Gallup polls show 'great deal/quite a lot of trust' in scientists fell from ~70% (early 2020s) to ~55-60% (mid-2020s). The drivers:
answer: COVID policy reversals, replication crisis revelations, perception of political influence in scientific institutions
choices: COVID policy reversals, replication crisis revelations, perception of political influence in scientific institutions
Trust in science has actually risen continuously since 2000 and is now at historical highs in all surveys
Trust in science is unmeasurable; no survey data exists on the topic in the United States or elsewhere
Public has unanimous trust in science with no decline in any measurable metric whatsoever ever observed
context: The political polarization of trust in science is striking — Democrats maintain high trust; Republicans and independents have substantially declined. The 'Trust the Science' framing during COVID may have backfired; making 'science' a brand demanding trust rather than a method of inquiry. The replication crisis has been concentrated in some fields (psychology, social science) but spilled over. The challenge: rebuilding trust requires acknowledgment of past errors and institutional reform. The current trajectory is concerning for democratic societies that depend on shared epistemic foundations.

question: Jay Bhattacharya, on March 25, 2025, was confirmed as the 18th Director of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) on a 53-47 Senate vote. The institutional context:
answer: Same agency where Francis Collins's 2020 FOIA emails called him 'fringe' — full institutional vindication
choices: Same agency where Francis Collins's 2020 FOIA emails called him 'fringe' — full institutional vindication
Bhattacharya rejected the nomination and chose to remain at Stanford instead of accepting NIH role
Bhattacharya has no academic credentials and was unable to receive nomination from any administration ever
Bhattacharya was unanimously confirmed by 100-0 vote with strong support from all Senators of both parties
context: Bhattacharya's confirmation marks a major institutional shift. The agency that had three years earlier marshaled resources against him (Collins's email calling for 'quick and devastating takedown' of GBD) is now under his leadership. He has announced research-integrity reforms, focus on chronic disease research, and reform of NIH's grant-making processes. In February 2026, he was concurrently appointed Acting CDC Director. His trajectory parallels other previously-dissenting scientists' rehabilitation. Whether his agenda produces beneficial reforms or harmful disruptions will be evaluated over coming years.

question: The 'Right to Try' federal law (signed May 30, 2018) followed by ~40 state laws granted terminally ill patients access to experimental drugs after Phase 1 trials. The FDA opposition:
answer: Argued patients should use existing compassionate-use pathway; libertarian supporters argued patient autonomy is paramount
choices: Argued patients should use existing compassionate-use pathway; libertarian supporters argued patient autonomy is paramount
FDA fully supported the Right to Try law and helped draft the federal legislation in 2018 administratively
FDA has actively worked to expand Right to Try beyond its original scope to all medical drugs always
The Right to Try federal law was never actually enacted; references to it are media fabrications historically
context: Goldwater Institute had advocated for Right to Try for ~6 years before federal passage. The FDA's resistance reflected institutional preference for centralized control. The law has been used by hundreds of patients but uptake has been modest. The underlying philosophical question — when is regulatory authority justified vs. when does individual liberty take precedence in life-and-death decisions — remains contested. The law's existence is part of the broader libertarian-vs-regulatory debate that shapes US health policy. Whether outcomes have been beneficial or harmful is debated.

question: An animal that eats only plants is what kind of consumer?
answer: Herbivore
context: Herbivores eat plants. Carnivores eat meat. Omnivores eat both.

question: A plant uses sunlight to make food. What role does the plant play in the food chain?
answer: Producer
context: Producers make their own food. Consumers eat producers or other consumers.

question: Worms and fungi break down dead leaves into soil. What role do they play?
answer: Decomposers
context: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead matter back into the soil.

question: Owls eat mice that eat grain. The owls and mice are linked in what?
answer: A food chain
context: A food chain shows who eats whom in a habitat.

question: Energy flows up a food chain, but most is lost as heat at each level. About what fraction passes to the next?
answer: About one tenth
context: The 10% rule: roughly 90% of energy is used or lost as heat at each trophic level.

question: A keystone species has an impact much larger than its numbers would suggest. Which is a textbook example?
answer: Sea otters in kelp forests
context: Sea otters eat sea urchins. Without otters, urchins eat kelp forests bare.

question: Two species that occupy nearly the same niche cannot coexist for long. What is this idea called?
answer: Competitive exclusion
context: Gause's principle: one species will out-compete the other or shift niches.

question: Wolves return to Yellowstone, elk herds shrink, willows regrow, and rivers shift course. This chain effect is a what?
answer: Trophic cascade
context: A top predator changes prey behavior, which changes plant life, which changes the landscape.
